notes: Paul A. David, «The Dynamo and the Computer», American Economic Review, 1990.
In 1899 electric motors were under 5% of US factory drive power. Until about 1920 most factories added motors to the old shaft-and-belt system and kept the old layout.
Productivity jumped only in the 1920s, about 40 years after the first power station, once one motor per machine let factories be rebuilt around the flow of work.
His data's lesson: the gains came from redesigning the work, not from adding the motor.
David himself warns against pushing the analogy too far; say so if asked.
